fig10_relations.how_to_read: A: the relations between the papers' measures and Panjabi's, nine in the README and ten markers since the body section's box is drawn with and without its convex bound, as the share of table C's synthetic vertebrae failing each, filled circles the generator, open squares C's nearest point; the within, past, outside and positive relations no anatomy can fail, the box and convex bounds hold under allowances. B: the unions by table, from sign or inside through necessary to any, solid lines the generator, dotted the nearest point, circles table A, squares B, triangles C. Good: the necessary markers in A and the necessary union in B near zero; a box bound read as an area drawn apart from the extents that bound it.
fig10_relations.what_it_shows: On table C at the generator 15.5% of vertebrae and 96% of people fail a relation no anatomy can fail, and the nearest point lowers that only to 12.4% and 78%. The failures sit where two papers' means are drawn independently: the medial cortex and the inner width against the pedicle's width fail 19.5%, and Griffith's body section passes Moncada's rectangle in 30.2%. On table B alone the necessary union is 12.5%, so independent draws, not disagreement between the papers, make the impossible vertebrae.

fig11_state_space_all.how_to_read: Each panel moves one axis from the generator's point and reads the result on three tables drawn from their own means and SDs: A Panjabi's every measure (circles), B the papers' (squares), C both (triangles). A: the true SD over the table's own, the dotted line at 1 self-consistency; B: the share failing a necessary relation; C: the neighbouring-level correlation against rho; D: any indicator but the floor against the size's spread. The large grey marker, in each table's shape, is that table's nearest point of the 480-point grid, placed at its own value of the panel's axis, beside or off the line. Good: grey on the line of 1 in A, below the black lines in B and D.
fig11_state_space_all.what_it_shows: Each table drawn from its own numbers reads a true SD 1.11 to 1.25 times its own at the generator's point and 1.00 or 1.01 at its nearest point, which for every table sits at sd_scale 1.0, scale_sd 0 or 0.01, rho 0.9 and r_between 0.4. The SD ratio is self-consistency, not a fit to the papers, whose SDs set sd_scale at 0.6, though the grid is still scored partly by Griffith's four correlations. At those points the necessary failures fall from 6.0, 12.4 and 15.4% to 5.7, 10.9 and 12.9% on A, B and C.

fig12_naming_measures.how_to_read: A is the whole column C3 to L5, B the lumbar run L1 to L5; along the bottom how many measures of table C the exact rule reads, from the seven SPINEPS measures through the generator's 32 to every complete measure; up the side the share of synthetic fields named exactly. Triangles, squares and circles are fields of one, three and nine bodies (five in B); solid lines are columns drawn at the generator's point, dotted at C's nearest grid point, a self-consistency reading the legend names nearest the papers (C). Good: a steep climb from the seven to the 32, then flat.
fig12_naming_measures.what_it_shows: More measures name more fields exactly: at the generator's point one body of the whole column is named exactly in 47.3% of fields on the seven measures, 87.2% on the 32 and 89.0% on all 35; three bodies in 72.8, 98.3 and 98.9%. Over the lumbar run one body reads 49.1% on the seven and 97.6% on C's 62. From 32 measures on the two points read alike at three bodies, and the answers at 0.99 are right 97 to 100% of the time.

fig13_spread_all.how_to_read: Every measure the papers pool from three series or more, widest spread at the left; each grey point is a cell, the REML tau between series over the cell's SD, so the axis reads in units of one person's spread; the large marker is the measure's median, filled for one of Panjabi's, open for one the papers alone report. The dotted line at 1 is where the series differ by exactly a person's SD; a measure the papers agree on sits well below it.
fig13_spread_all.what_it_shows: The published series disagree by about a person's SD: over 81 cells of 14 measures the median tau over SD is 1.07 (quartiles 0.72 to 1.38), 81% of cells over 0.5, less on the papers' own five measures (0.76) than on Panjabi's nine (1.15). Of the papers' own five measures the anterior body height is the widest at 1.61 and the mid body height the narrowest at 0.23; the widest of all, the pedicle's sagittal inclination at 2.78, is Panjabi's. By part A's rule an infinite pool of series is worth a median 0.1 scan for the inclination and 28 for the mid body height.

fig14_strata.how_to_read: A is a forest plot: one row a paper left out, its loss in points of fields named exactly at three bodies over L1 to L5 against a rule built on its own table, under the rule built on the other papers (filled circles), the same rule with every SD widened by tau (open squares) and its own means under the others' SD (small triangles, the SD difference alone), bars 95% intervals; the top rows are the pooled losses with the interval for one more population. B is the pooled loss by field width; C the share of answers at 0.99 that are right, the mean over the populations with the whisker down to the worst, the dotted line at 99; D the loss on eight populations drawn from the model. Good: losses near zero, every mark at 99 or above in C.
fig14_strata.what_it_shows: A rule built on the other papers loses a pooled 8.8 points at one body and 12.2 at three against a paper's own table, with a spread between papers of 6.7 to 8.4 points, so one more population may lose anything from nothing to about 30; the SD difference alone costs 2 to 4 of those points, the shift of the means the rest. Widening by tau names nothing better (a paired 0.2 points or less) but answers at 0.99 half as often; over the answers it is right on 88% against 89% at three bodies, both floors Yadav 2020's, whose printed SDs are twice the pool's, and Yadav apart on 99% against 96%, on the pedicle pair 98% against 96%, and on populations drawn from the model 100% against 86%.

fig1_means.how_to_read: One lumbar measure per panel, L1 to L5 along the bottom, millimetres up the side. Black circles are Panjabi's means, which the generator draws around; open squares with bars are the papers pooled, triangles where only one or two series exist; the grey band is the synthetic mean plus or minus one SD. Good: each black circle inside the square's bars. The band is the generator's own spread, held to the papers' SDs in the next figure, not to the scatter of the circles, which are series means.
fig1_means.what_it_shows: In his own SDs, Tan's series left out, Panjabi's means sit above the pooled papers in the two depths (1.3 and 1.4) and the pedicle (0.8 and 1.0), within 0.4 in the end-plate's width, the canal's width and its area, and 1.96 below in the posterior body height; the squares drawn here pool Tan too, which pulls the canal's cells down. Over the 57 cells pooled from three or more series his mean never leaves the prediction interval, so his twelve spines are a plausible, large population. The band, the generator's measured spread, is a median 1.71 times the papers' SD over lengths and areas.

fig2_spread.how_to_read: Panel A, one column per measure on a log scale: each cell's synthetic SD over the pooled published SD, the median over levels with a bar from the first to the third quartile; the dotted line at 1 is the papers' own spread. Filled circles are the generator, open squares its SDs with the size taken out, open triangles the nearest point to the papers, open diamonds Panjabi's own SDs. B is the same by level. Good: markers on the dotted line.
fig2_spread.what_it_shows: The synthetic spread is about 70% too wide: over 140 cells the generator's true-anatomy SD is a median 1.71 times the papers' (1.86 as measured). Most of the excess is inherited: Panjabi's twelve spines' SDs are already 1.51 times the papers', 2.83 for the angles, and the generator then multiplies them by a size of its own. The nearest point, every SD at 0.6 of his, brings the ratio to 0.98.

fig3_structure.how_to_read: A: the correlation between pairs of measures over L1 to L5, the x Griffith's 1,080 CTs, the filled circle the generator, the square and triangle two other settings; good is a circle on the x. B: each measure's share of the body's sex difference, the dashed line at 1 the generator, which scales every measure alike. C and D: two ratios by level, the grey band synthetic, open markers the papers; good is papers inside the band.
fig3_structure.what_it_shows: The generator ties the canal to the body more than Griffith does (0.56 to 0.59 against his 0.24 to 0.48) and the canal's depth to its width less (0.50 against 0.58), because one size scales every length alike. The papers do not scale alike either: Eisenstein's skeletons put the canal's width at 0.35 of the body's sex difference and its depth at 0.00. By level the synthetic ratios are Panjabi's shape, within 0.03, and sit below Alonge 2021's and Cizmic 2023's.

fig4_state_space.how_to_read: A to E move one axis of the generator at a time, the others held at its own point (circled): the SD ratio against the size's spread and the SDs' scale, the neighbouring-level correlation against rho, Griffith's correlations against r_between, the flagged share against the SDs' scale. F is the grid search, the distance from the papers against sd_scale, one line per scale_sd, the star the nearest point. Good: a star at the bottom of a bowl in F, which pins the SDs' scale on this slice; a line still falling at the grid's edge leaves that axis open.
fig4_state_space.what_it_shows: The nearest of 480 points takes every SD to 0.6 of Panjabi's, halves the size's spread and sets rho 0.9 and r_between 0.2, at a distance of 0.023: the true SD ratio reads 0.98 against 1.70 at the generator, and the flagged vertebrae fall from 42% to 7%. Only the SDs' scale is pinned, to 0.6 to 0.7; the size's spread, rho and r_between stay open, since Griffith's four correlations are one constraint on all three.

fig5_naming.how_to_read: A, B and C are fields of one, three and nine bodies; along the bottom the points of the state space, the generator at the left and the nearest point at the right; up the side the share of fields the exact rule on the seven SPINEPS measures names exactly, bars 95% intervals over 300 columns. Filled circles are the generator's rule applied everywhere, open squares a rule that knows the setting. Higher is better; a small gap between circle and square means the rule loses little by not knowing the setting.
fig5_naming.what_it_shows: The nearest point names better than the generator at every width: one body in 57.1% of fields against 47.5%, three in 80.2% against 72.8%, nine in 99.0% against 95.6%. Doubling the CT's error costs most, 8 points at one body; a narrower population gains 9 to 11 points; phi and r_between cost almost nothing. The gaps say which axes the rule is sensitive to, nothing about real patients.

fig6_power.how_to_read: A repeats part B: each circle a cell's spread between published series over Panjabi's SD, the solid line the median 0.83, the dashed line part B's 0.39. B and C score the exact rule on tables moved by that disagreement, against bodies seen: the points of exact naming lost, and how often answers at 0.99 are right. D to F put whole spines on a log axis, the dotted line at the 159 gold persons: the least shift, the least SD ratio and the columns expected with each anomaly. Good: near 0 in B, near 100 in C, steep lines in D and E.
fig6_power.what_it_shows: The papers disagree by a median 0.83 of Panjabi's SD over 57 cells, 2.1 times the 0.39 part B read, and a rule built on a table moved by that much loses 10 to 20 points, its answers at 0.99 right only 88 to 96% of the time. At 159 whole spines a test finds a shift of 0.22 SD and an SD ratio of 1.17 against the table taken as exact, but only 1.36 SD and 1.81 against Panjabi's twelve as the sample they are.

fig7_quality.how_to_read: A: the share of synthetic vertebrae each indicator flags at the generator (filled circles), with the size taken out of Panjabi's SDs (squares) and at the nearest point (triangles), the three unions at the right. B: the box indicator by level for the generator, canal and end-plate areas apart. C: the canal's shape factor, its area over width times depth, the grey band the generator's SD, Tan 2004's ratio as diamonds, the dotted line the bound. D: the three unions with box and convex, by phenotype. Good: lines near zero in A, a band under the bound in C, flat lines in D.
fig7_quality.what_it_shows: 42.2% of synthetic vertebrae and 9,998 of 10,000 people carry a flag at the generator, most for an area larger than its own rectangle (box, 32.3%), then an end-plate under half of it (convex, 10.5%); sign and inside, which no anatomy can fail, flag 2.2%. Taking the size out of Panjabi's SDs brings the union to 25.4%, the nearest point to 7.1%; the six phenotypes carry the same rates. Curation is counted, never applied.

fig8_assumptions.how_to_read: A: the generator's 1 mm error of one reading, the dashed line, against the error SD each paper reports, one circle per figure with a bar over its range, labelled by what was measured and on what. B, on a log scale: how often each anomaly is assumed (squares, model.py; diamonds, the chain of levels) against how often the papers count it (circles with 95% intervals). Good: the dashed line inside the bars in A, squares and diamonds inside the circles' intervals in B.
fig8_assumptions.what_it_shows: The generator's 1 mm error is larger than most of the papers' reading errors, which run 0.20 to 0.65 mm for body heights and pedicles on CT and 0.35 to 0.95 mm for the pedicle by caliper. Its anomaly shares are 4 to 9 times the papers' counts: model.py draws each phenotype in one column in six (16.7%) where Eisenstein's 443 skeletons count six lumbar-type segments in 2.48% and Duman's 517 CTs a missing twelfth rib in 4.26%, and no paper counts a thirteenth rib-bearing body.

fig9_tables.how_to_read: A: the 106 keys of the reread's vocabulary by fate, the bars summing to the vocabulary. B: the measures each table holds a cell for at each level C3 to L5, circles table A (Panjabi), squares B (the papers), triangles C (both); a flat line covers the spine evenly. C: the papers' cells at each level stacked by where the SD comes from, pooled from two or more series, one series, or Tan 2004 alone, whose SD is uncertain. The panel shows how many of each level's cells rest on an uncertain SD, one series or a pooled SD.
fig9_tables.what_it_shows: Of the vocabulary's 95 measures of a vertebra, 68 are drawn in some table: A holds Panjabi's 42 in 782 cells, B the papers' 53 in 694 cells, C both, 75 in 1,054. But 292 of the papers' 694 cells rest on Tan's uncertain SD alone, 279 on one other series and only 123 on a pooled SD. The papers measure the lumbar spine far more than the rest, 51 to 53 measures at L1 to L5 against 22 at C3.

render1_axial.how_to_read: L3 from above, anterior up: the large outline is the upper end-plate, the hatched section the canal between the pedicle walls, the bars the transverse processes, the stem the spinous process, a scale bar under each. A is Panjabi's means; B, C and D are three synthetic people. A section is dashed where no superellipse of its width and depth holds its area (box) and draws as a diamond when the area is under half its box (convex). Good: a synthetic vertebra that looks like A.
render1_axial.what_it_shows: B passes every indicator and draws close to Panjabi's means; C and D show the two commonest flags. C's canal area is 107% of its own width-by-depth box, nearly Panjabi's area (271 against 280 mm2) inside a smaller box, so it is dashed; D's upper end-plate holds 0.47 of its box against Panjabi's 0.77, so it draws as a diamond. On the whole draw these flags take 32.3% and 10.5% of vertebrae, and the vertebrae failing any indicator fall from 42% to 7% at the nearest point.

render2_column.how_to_read: The lumbar column from in front, L1 at the top, each body a rectangle of its end-plate width by its posterior height, the canal hatched over it, the transverse span a thin line, one scale for all three panels. A is Panjabi's means; B the synthetic person whose L3 passes every indicator and sits nearest his means; C the one whose L3 canal passes its own rectangle by the median excess. A heavy outline marks a flagged body, the flag named. Good: bodies widening steadily from L1 to L5 and no heavy outline.
render2_column.what_it_shows: Even the person picked for an L3 that passes carries a box flag at L2, as 9,998 of 10,000 synthetic people carry at least one. The shapes show why: Panjabi's end-plate widths rise steadily from 41.2 mm at L1 to 47.3 at L5, while the boxed person's run 38.8, 36.2, 38.7, 42.5 and 35.9 mm, out of order with L5 the narrowest, since the generator draws each measure from an SD a median 1.71 times the papers' and ties every length to one size.

render3_solid.how_to_read: Three lumbar columns as solids, seen from the left and behind, shaded from one light. A is Panjabi's means; B and C are two synthetic people of the first drawing. Each body is lofted between the superellipses of its two end-plates, so what differs between the panels is the bodies' proportions and the column's height; the pedicles, laminae and processes are boxes of fixed thickness. Good: five bodies in proportion from L1 to L5, none that pinches or flares between its plates as C's L3 does.
render3_solid.what_it_shows: B's L3 passes every indicator; its upper end-plate, 44.7 by 34.0 mm with 1,211 mm2, sits beside Panjabi's 44.1 by 35.2 with 1,194. C's L3 fails two: its upper plate holds 886 mm2, under half its 47.5 by 39.3 rectangle (convex), and its lower plate 1,775 mm2, past its 42.7 by 27.8 rectangle (box), so it is drawn as the box. The drawn heights, 144 mm for Panjabi's means, 129 for B and 160 for C, show the size the generator draws on top of his SDs.

fig15_select.how_to_read: A and B: each candidate rule along the bottom, the paper's own table first as the ceiling; up the side the held-out log loss (A, lower is better) and exact naming (B), the mean over the 22 papers held out with bars one SE, one line per field width. C: the calibration curve at three bodies, every field of every population pooled, the posterior's top probability against the share named right; the dotted line is perfect, and ECE the expected calibration error. D and E: the held-out log loss along the SD factor and the temperature, the ticks the values the inner leave-one-out chose. F: the winner's log score minus the plain rule's on each population at three bodies, bars 95%.
fig15_select.what_it_shows: Tempering by T = 2 has the lowest held-out log loss at every width, 0.09 to 0.12 nats below the plain rule and better on 15 to 17 of 22 populations, with the calibration error down from 0.10 to 0.02 to 0.04, and names exactly what the plain rule names; half of its mean gain is Yadav 2020's. The widened rule is second with no knob. No candidate names more than half a point better (the mixture, within its SE), and none closes the gap to the paper's own table. The inner choices sit where the held-out curves bottom, at k = 1.45 and T = 2.

fig16_exclusion.how_to_read: A and B: each exclusion candidate down the side, its held-out log score (A, right is better) and exact naming (B) minus the plain rule's, paired over the 22 populations, bars one SE, one marker a field width. C: each held-out population at three bodies, the three untempered candidates' log score minus plain. D: the calibration error of every candidate, all populations pooled.
fig16_exclusion.what_it_shows: Leaving Yadav 2020 out is 0.04 to 0.05 nats worse than plain and costs Front. Phys. 2026's population 0.81 nats; leaving Front. Phys. 2026 out costs Busscher, Moncada-Habib and Tan 0.16 to 0.21; one vote per population is within 0.006 of plain. Tempered, all are within 0.012 nats of the tempered plain rule, so no paper leaves the prior.

fig17_covariates.how_to_read: A: men minus women in within-sex SDs (Hedges' g), each paper's own men against its own women, papers pooled, 95% intervals, the papers named. B: the same for age per decade and body height and weight, from each paper's own bands. C: the AUC of telling men from women by one measure at one level, one dot a printed stratum, filled in the population, open held out. D: the share of a measure's variance sex or age explains, the population's own split and held out.
fig17_covariates.what_it_shows: Sex moves the end plate by 1.4 to 1.6 SDs (Chen 2011) and the disc heights by 0.3 to 0.8 (Bach 2019); age moves a measure by under a quarter of an SD a decade; body height moves the pedicle by 0.34 to 0.48 SD per 100 mm (Yu 2015). Held out, the direction of the sex effect transfers between Bach and Twomey and its size does not.

fig_tan_strata.how_to_read: A: in the seven measures' matched cells, the rest's series, the interval for one more population from the merged pool and from the rest alone (t, and the spread taken as known), and Tan 2004's mean. B: the rule's loss on each stratum's tables, quick record. C: each interval's leave-one-out coverage against its width.
fig_tan_strata.what_it_shows: Tan sits a median 1.71 of Panjabi's SD below the rest; apart, the spread between populations falls from 0.87 to 0.63 SD and the rule's naming moves by under a point. The plug-in interval covers held-out series 87% of the time, Higgins' t interval 96 to 100% (the Tan thread's reading, README answer 8).

fig_subgroups.how_to_read: A: the share of the spread between populations each register variable accounts for, a dot a cell, bars the median with Tan 2004 in (black) and out (grey). B and C: each paper and each value against the rest, Tan filled. D: differences a paper prints apart, the sexes within age bands and two ancestries of one collection.
fig_subgroups.what_it_shows: With Tan out the variables account for almost none of the spread between papers (decade, modality and age band 0.00, country 0.35); only the specimen holds (0.24). The within-paper contrasts are few: Duman's men 0.07 to 0.21 SD wider pedicles, Yu's ancestries -0.23 to 0.20 SD (the Tan thread's reading, README answer 9).
